title: Chris Kercher on why his new law firm will need far fewer lawyers
excerpt: After 17 years at Quinn Emanuel, Christopher Kercher is building a law firm around the idea that AI can help lawyers offer faster, cheaper service.
content_html:
The law firm of the future may look less like a pyramid — and more like an obelisk

By Melia Robinson

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

After 17 years at Quinn Emanuel, Christopher Kercher began building his new law firm from the line for Big Thunder Mountain Railroad at Disney World.

With Claude on his phone, he cruised through some of the chores that come with starting a firm. Five years ago, Kercher said, the sheer hassle might have persuaded him to give up. Artificial intelligence removed enough of the friction to make striking out on his own feel possible.

Now, Kercher is betting the technology can do something more ambitious: change the shape of the law firm itself.

At Kercher Law, he plans to take on the high-stakes corporate disputes that defined his practice at Quinn Emanuel, one of the world's largest litigation firms. He expects to do the work with far fewer lawyers.

For generations, large law firms have been structured like pyramids. At the bottom, junior lawyers sift through documents, research the law, and write first drafts. Their work travels through progressively smaller layers of senior associates before reaching the lead partner, who makes the important calls.

Each handoff adds judgment. It also adds time — and another line to the bill.

Kercher is building a law firm around the idea that artificial intelligence can shrink some of those layers. He expects to employ no more than "low double digits" of attorneys. At launch, he is the firm's sole trial lawyer, supported by a small team handling technology and operations.

"I am not going to rebuild the pyramid," Kercher said.

Instead, he expects the firm to look more like an obelisk (think the Washington Monument). It would stand lean from bottom to top, with experienced lawyers working more directly with the software systems that gather facts and crank out drafts.

Kercher is part of a small but growing group of lawyers walking away from Big Law to build "AI-native" firms. They are betting that boutiques can adopt new tools faster than large firms, where software can spend months winding through red tape.

The experiment comes with regulatory and ethical questions, however. These firms must show they can try new ways of practicing law without cutting corners on the rules of the profession.

For clients, Kercher argues, a small firm's edge goes beyond a smaller bill. Large teams impose what he calls a "coordination tax." Lawyers spend time bringing one another up to speed, while facts and nuance can get lost as work moves from associates to partners.

The model also lets Kercher offer clients different ways to get legal help. He has begun holding standing monthly meetings for a flat fee, using the conversations to learn the business. When a dispute comes up, Kercher said he can reach a view faster about whether the claim is worth fighting, settling, or heading off entirely.

That speed depends on giving bots more of the work that once flowed through associates. Kercher relies on broad-use AI tools ChatGPT and Claude rather than software specifically built for lawyers. He uses them to turn sprawling sets of emails, contracts, and other records into timelines and to organize his thinking about how the facts and characters fit together.

He has also built a Claude skill that plays opposing counsel, probing his arguments for weaknesses before the other side gets the chance.

That digital adversary is part of a broader experiment. How much can one litigator accomplish with an army of digital coworkers?

Kercher did not bring any Quinn Emanuel partners with him. He said the solo launch was deliberate. Before building out the firm's human ranks, he wants to see how far technology can extend his reach — and where another lawyer can add something Claude cannot.

content_html_zh:
未来的律师事务所可能看起来不太像金字塔，而更像方尖碑

作者：Melia Robinson 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

在 Quinn Emanuel 工作了 17 年后，Christopher Kercher 开始在迪士尼世界的大雷山铁路沿线建立他的新律师事务所。

克劳德一边打电话，一边浏览着创办公司的一些琐事。 克尔彻说，五年前，纯粹的麻烦可能让他放弃了。 人工智能消除了足够多的摩擦，让他感觉自己的创业成为可能。

现在，Kercher 认为这项技术可以做一些更雄心勃勃的事情：改变律师事务所本身的形态。

在 Kercher Law，他计划处理高风险的公司纠纷，这些纠纷定义了他在 Quinn Emanuel（全球最大的诉讼公司之一）的业务。 他希望用更少的律师来完成这项工作。

几代人以来，大型律师事务所的结构就像金字塔一样。 在底层，初级律师筛选文件、研究法律并撰写初稿。 他们的工作会先经过越来越小的高级合伙人层级，然后才到达负责做出重要决定的首席合伙人。

每次交接都会增加判断力。 它还增加了时间——以及账单上的另一行。

Kercher 正在围绕人工智能可以缩小其中一些层面的想法建立一家律师事务所。 他预计聘用的律师人数不会超过“低两位数”。 成立之初，他是该公司唯一的出庭律师，并由负责技术和运营的小团队提供支持。

“我不会重建金字塔，”克尔彻说。

相反，他希望该公司看起来更像一座方尖碑（想想华盛顿纪念碑）。 它将自下而上保持精简，经验丰富的律师更直接地与收集事实和起草草稿的软件系统合作。

Kercher 是一个规模虽小但不断壮大的律师群体中的一员，他们放弃了 Big Law 并建立了“人工智能原生”公司。 他们押注精品店能够比大公司更快地采用新工具，而大公司的软件可能需要花费数月时间才能完成繁文缛节。

然而，该实验存在监管和伦理问题。 这些公司必须证明他们可以尝试新的法律执业方式，而不会在行业规则上走捷径。

克尔彻认为，对于客户来说，小公司的优势不仅仅在于较小的账单。 大型团队征收他所谓的“协调税”。 律师们花时间互相通报最新情况，而随着工作从合伙人转移到合伙人，事实和细微差别可能会丢失。

该模式还让 Kercher 为客户提供不同的方式来获得法律帮助。 他开始每月举行固定费用的常设会议，通过对话来了解业务。 克尔彻表示，当出现争议时，他可以更快地判断该索赔是否值得抗争、解决或完全停止。

这种速度取决于让机器人承担更多曾经由同事完成的工作。 Kercher 依赖于广泛使用的人工智能工具 ChatGPT 和 Claude，而不是专门为律师构建的软件。 他利用它们将大量的电子邮件、合同和其他记录转化为时间线，并组织他对事实和人物如何结合在一起的思考。

他还培养了克劳德的技能，可以扮演对方的律师，在对方有机会之前探究他的论点的弱点。

这个数字对手是更广泛实验的一部分。 一位诉讼律师在一群数字化同事的帮助下能完成多少工作？

克尔彻没有带来任何奎因·伊曼纽尔合伙人。 他说单独推出是经过深思熟虑的。 在建立公司的人员队伍之前，他想看看技术可以将他的影响力扩大到什么程度，以及其他律师可以在哪些方面添加克劳德无法做到的内容。
